feed.title: Arxo Findings Register
feed.subtitle: Verified discrepancies in legal texts, standards, official publications and implementations, with evidence and correction histories.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0454 — Rome II on EUR-Lex: the XHTML text lacks two of the three Commission statements printed in the Official Journal
entry.summary: Reported. The Official Journal prints three Commission statements after Rome II: on the review clause, on road accidents and on the treatment of foreign law. The English and French PDFs contain all three. The XHTML manifestations in Cellar contain only the statement on the review clause in 23 languages; the Croatian XHTML contains all three.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0453 — Rome II: which event must a choice of law follow under Article 14(1)(a) when several events give rise to the damage?
entry.summary: Reported. Article 14(1)(a) allows a choice by an agreement entered into after the event giving rise to the damage. Where several events give rise to the damage, for example a first act in one country and a final act in another, and the parties are not all pursuing a commercial activity, the text does not say which event the agreement must follow.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0452 — Rome II: at what time is foreseeability assessed under Article 5(1), second subparagraph?
entry.summary: Reported. The law of the habitual residence of the person claimed to be liable applies if that person could not reasonably foresee the marketing of the product. The text does not say whether foreseeability is assessed when the product was put on the market, when it was marketed in that country, or when the damage occurred.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0451 — Rome I: where is a service supplied at a distance, for Article 6(4)(a)?
entry.summary: Reported. Article 6(4)(a) takes out of the consumer rules services to be supplied to the consumer exclusively in a country other than that of his habitual residence. For a service supplied at a distance, for example online advice used by the consumer at home, the text does not say where the service is supplied.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0450 — Rome I: which Member State prevails when two Member States impose conflicting compulsory insurance on the same risk?
entry.summary: Reported. Point (a) of Article 7(4) gives priority to the law of the Member State imposing the obligation to take out insurance, and point (b) lets each such State require the contract to be governed by its law. The two points do not say which of two such States prevails when their rules conflict.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0449 — Rome II, Hungarian and Danish versions: does the review clause ask for more than the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. The Hungarian and Danish texts of Article 30(1) add a sentence that the other versions do not have: the report shall in particular examine non-contractual obligations arising out of traffic accidents and violations of privacy and rights relating to personality, including defamation.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0448 — Rome II, Bulgarian version: does Article 22(2) cover the same acts as the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions cover acts intended to have legal effect. The Bulgarian text covers unilateral declarations of will with legal effects.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0447 — Rome II, Romanian and Lithuanian versions: does Article 15 describe the same matters as the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. In Article 15(d) the Romanian text speaks of protective measures where the other versions speak of the measures a court may take to prevent or stop injury or damage. In Article 15(h) the Lithuanian text names acquisitive prescription, which concerns property, beside the limitation of actions.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0446 — Rome II, Dutch and Romanian versions: does Article 23 define habitual residence in the same way as the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. In the second subparagraph of Article 23(1) the Dutch text names a subsidiary, a branch or another establishment where the other versions name a branch, an agency or any other establishment. In Article 23(2) the Romanian text replaces a natural person acting in the course of his or her business activity with activity during working hours.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0445 — Rome II, Croatian and Slovenian versions: must all the parties pursue a commercial activity for a choice under Article 14(1)(b)?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions allow a freely negotiated choice before the event where all the parties pursue a commercial activity. The Croatian and Slovenian texts say both parties.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0444 — Rome II, Croatian version: does Article 4(2) apply to the person claimed to be liable or only to a person whose liability is established?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions apply the common habitual residence rule to the person claimed to be liable. The Croatian text speaks of the person whose liability has been established.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0443 — Rome II, Bulgarian and Slovenian versions: does Article 6(3)(b) set the same conditions as the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. Article 6(3)(b) lets the claimant rely on the law of the court where the market is affected in more than one country, if the market in that Member State is directly and substantially affected. The Bulgarian text says more than one Member State; the Slovenian text says directly or substantially.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0442 — Rome I and Rome II, Danish, Italian and Romanian versions: does the rule on multiple liability require joint and several liability?
entry.summary: Reported. Most versions apply the rule to several debtors liable for the same claim. The Danish and Italian texts of both Regulations, and the Romanian text of Rome I, say jointly and severally liable. The Romanian text of Rome II says liable together.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0441 — Rome I, five versions: are multilateral trading systems in Article 4(1)(h) defined by non-discretionary rules?
entry.summary: Reported. Article 4(1)(h) covers contracts in a multilateral system that brings together interests in financial instruments in accordance with non-discretionary rules. The Lithuanian, Greek, Maltese and Hungarian texts say non-discriminatory; the Danish text says mandatory.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0440 — Rome I, six versions: does Article 7(3) limit the choice for mass risks to the law of a Member State?
entry.summary: Reported. In points (a) and (c) of Article 7(3) most versions limit the choice for mass-risk insurance to the law of a Member State. The Slovak, Dutch and Finnish texts of point (a) and the Swedish, Estonian and Slovenian texts of point (c) speak of a country or state.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0439 — Rome I, Latvian and Estonian versions: does the escape clause for large-risk insurance require a clear and manifest closer connection?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions require that it is clear from all the circumstances that the contract is manifestly more closely connected with another country. The Latvian text has no word for clear or manifestly; the Estonian text keeps clearly but not manifestly.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0438 — Rome I, Croatian and Dutch versions: does the escape clause for employment contracts set the same test as the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions ask whether the contract is more closely connected with another country. The Croatian text asks for the closest connection; the Dutch text asks for a manifestly closer connection, and no other version has manifestly in this paragraph.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0437 — Rome II, Croatian version: Articles 5(1) and 9 refer to Article 42(2), and Rome II has 32 articles
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions of Article 5(1) (product liability) and Article 9 (industrial action) begin without prejudice to Article 4(2), the rule on common habitual residence. The Croatian text refers to Article 42(2). There is no Croatian corrigendum to Rome II.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0436 — Rome I, Latvian version: does Article 11(1) on formal validity cover persons in the same country, as in the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions cover in paragraph 1 a contract between persons in the same country and in paragraph 2 persons in different countries. In the Latvian text both paragraphs cover persons in different countries.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0435 — Rome I, Danish version: Article 7(3) refers to paragraph 3 instead of Article 3, so the paragraph refers to itself
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions say that the parties may choose one of the listed laws in accordance with Article 3 (freedom of choice). The Danish text says in accordance with paragraph 3, the paragraph in which the words stand.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0434 — Rome I, Irish version: is a large-risk insurance contract without a choice governed by the law of the consumer or of the insurer?
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions point to the law of the country where the insurer has his habitual residence. The Irish text names the consumer, a party that a large-risk insurance contract does not have.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0433 — Rome I, Maltese version: Article 8(4) refers to paragraph 2 or 2a, and there is no paragraph 2a
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions of the escape clause for employment contracts refer to paragraphs 2 or 3. Article 8 has no paragraph 2a.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0432 — Rome I, Croatian version: does Article 8(2) on employment contracts apply in the absence of a choice of law, as in the other versions?
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions open paragraph 2 with the absence of a choice by the parties. The Croatian opening repeats the condition of paragraph 3 and makes paragraph 2 depend on paragraph 2 itself. Croatian corrigenda 32008R0593R(04) and R(06) do not touch Article 8.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0431 — Rome II, Greek version: should Article 11(1) on negotiorum gestio refer to unjust enrichment, as the 2014 corrigendum made it?
entry.summary: Reported. The Greek corrigendum of 31 December 2014 replaced, in Article 11(1), the words with this non-contractual obligation by with that unjust enrichment. Article 11 is about negotiorum gestio, and the original Greek wording, like the other versions, tied the connection to that obligation. The same corrigendum also corrected Article 10(1), on unjust enrichment.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0429 — AI Act: which evaluation satisfies Article 82(1) when a compliant system presents only a risk to another public interest?
entry.summary: Reported. Article 82(1) applies, having performed an evaluation under Article 79, to a compliant high-risk AI system that presents a risk, including a risk to other aspects of public interest protection. Article 79(2) requires an evaluation for risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and Article 74(1) applies the general market surveillance framework of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. The text does not say which evaluation satisfies Article 82(1) where the only risk is to another public interest.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0428 — AI Act: is a voter exposed to the output of a campaign tool whose recommended messages staff send on?
entry.summary: Reported. Annex III, point 8(b), excludes AI systems to the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed. A campaign tool ranks voters and recommends which message each voter should receive; campaign staff then send those messages. The text does not say whether this counts as direct exposure to the output of the system, read with recital 62.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0427 — AI Act: which event starts the 10-year period of Articles 18(1) and 22(3)(b) when placing on the market and putting into service fall on different dates?
entry.summary: Reported. Articles 18(1) and 22(3)(b) count 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service. Where the two events happen on different dates, the text does not say which one starts the period.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0426 — AI Act, German and Estonian versions: Article 49(2) calls a system high-risk although the provider has concluded it is not
entry.summary: Reported. German and Estonian Article 49(2) call the object a high-risk system although the provider has concluded that it is not high-risk. The other versions say an AI system.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0425 — AI Act, Maltese version: Article 71(1) prints 6(40 for 6(4)
entry.summary: Reported. Maltese Article 71(1) refers to Article 6(40 where Article 6(4) is meant (a typing error).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0424 — AI Act, Article 112(6): “asses” for “assess”
entry.summary: Reported. Article 112(6), English version, reads asses the need.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0423 — AI Act, Article 111: “marked” for “market” in the title
entry.summary: Reported. The title of Article 111, English version, reads already placed on the marked.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0422 — AI Act, Article 101(1): missing word in “shall also into account”
entry.summary: Reported. The second subparagraph of Article 101(1), English version, reads The Commission shall also into account.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0421 — AI Act, Article 101(1): extra full stop before “when”
entry.summary: Reported. The first subparagraph of Article 101(1), English version, has an extra full stop in whichever is higher., when.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0420 — AI Act, Article 71(4): missing word in “accessible the public”
entry.summary: Reported. Article 71(4), English version, reads making the information accessible the public.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0419 — AI Act, Article 40(1): stray word in “set out in of Chapter V”
entry.summary: Reported. Article 40(1), English version, reads with the obligations set out in of Chapter V.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0418 — AI Act after the Digital Omnibus: Article 49(4)(b) still lists point 9 of Annex VIII, Section B, which was deleted
entry.summary: Reported. Article 1, point (42), of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deleted points 7 and 9 of Annex VIII, Section B. Article 49(4)(b) still lists points 8 and 9 of Section B. This has been noted publicly before.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0417 — AI Act, Annex VIII, Section C, point 5: the data protection impact assessment is referred to Article 26(8) instead of 26(9)
entry.summary: Reported. Article 26(8) is about registration by deployers that are public authorities. The data protection impact assessment is in Article 26(9). The error is in all 24 versions. This has been pointed out publicly before.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0416 — AI Act, Annex X: the quoted title of the Eurodac Regulation names Regulation (EU) 2024/1315 instead of 2024/1351
entry.summary: Reported. The title of Regulation (EU) 2024/1358 as published names Regulations (EU) 2024/1351 and (EU) 2024/1350. English and 22 other versions of Annex X have 2024/1315; the Finnish version has 2024/1351. The main reference to Regulation (EU) 2024/1358 is correct. The Spanish corrigendum of 4.5.2026 (OJ L, 2026/90343) restates Annex X, point 3, and keeps 2024/1315.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0414 — AI Act, Greek version: the first part of Article 74(8) refers to Annex III without limiting it to point 1
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions say listed in point 1 of Annex III. The limits to high-risk systems and to the stated purposes (law enforcement, border management, justice and democracy) remain. The second part (points 6, 7 and 8) is the same in all versions.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0413 — AI Act, Portuguese and Croatian versions: the 10^25 threshold of Article 51(2) is measured per second
entry.summary: Reported. The other 22 versions measure the cumulative amount of computation in floating point operations, without a time unit. The added words do not fit the cumulative quantity described in the same paragraph. Recital 111 and Annex XIII, point (c), support a total number of operations.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0411 — AI Act, Irish version: Article 113(b) does not except Article 101 from the date of 2 August 2025
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions add with the exception of Article 101. Read alone, the Irish wording includes Article 101 (fines for providers of general-purpose AI models) in the provisions applying from 2 August 2025.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0408 — AI Act, Italian version: Article 49(4)(a) lists registration fields 1 to 5, 8 and 9 instead of 1 to 5, 7 and 10
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions say points 1 to 10 of Annex VIII, Section A, with the exception of points 6, 8 and 9, that is points 1 to 5, 7 and 10. The Italian list includes points 8 and 9 (certificate details and a scanned copy of the certificate), which the other versions exclude. It leaves out point 7 (status of the system) and point 10 (Member States where the system is placed on the market, put into service or made available).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0407 — AI Act, Maltese version: Article 71(3) refers to Article 49(4) twice instead of Article 49(3) and (4)
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions refer to Article 49(3) and (4).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0406 — AI Act, Estonian version: Article 40(2) refers to Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 instead of Article 24
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions refer to Article 24 of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012, headed Reports. Article 2 of that Regulation contains definitions.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0405 — AI Act, Irish version: the definition of conformity assessment refers to a Title III that the Regulation does not have
entry.summary: Reported. The Irish text does not limit the reference to Section 2, and the Regulation has chapters, not titles. The other 23 versions keep the Section 2 reference: 22 refer to Chapter III, Section 2, and the German text says Titel III Abschnitt 2.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0404 — AI Act, Polish version: Article 41(5) refers to Chapter I, Section 2, which does not exist
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions refer to Section 2 of this Chapter, that is Chapter III, Section 2. Chapter I has no Section 2.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0403 — AI Act, Finnish version: technical documentation of general-purpose AI models refers to Annex IX instead of Annex XI
entry.summary: Reported. The other versions refer to Annex XI (technical documentation of general-purpose AI models). Annex IX is about registration of high-risk AI systems tested in real world conditions. The Finnish Annex XI itself refers back to Article 53(1)(a).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0402 — AI Act, Italian version: Article 71(1) refers to Article 69 where the other versions refer to Article 49
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions refer to Article 49 in this position. Article 69 is about access to the pool of experts by the Member States; registration is in Article 49.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0401 — AI Act, Maltese version: Article 73(7) refers to Article 3, point (44)(c), which does not exist
entry.summary: Reported. The other 23 versions refer to Article 3, point (49)(c): a serious incident that infringes obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights. Point (44) defines publicly accessible space and has no point (c). Maltese Article 3, point (49)(c), and the reference in Maltese Article 73(10) support the intended reading.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0400 — CRR: CAP30.23(4) vs CRR Art 72j(1)
entry.summary: Reported. Article 72j(1) CRR permits no deduction at exactly 5%, whereas Basel Framework CAP30.23(4) requires holdings to be less than 5%. The CRR does not provide discretion over this boundary.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0399 — Basel Framework: RBC25.9 FAQ3
entry.summary: Reported. RBC25.9 FAQ3 says an FX option hedging a banking book position is covered by RBC25.9(6), which only lists options on credit or equity risk from the bank's own issued instruments.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0398 — Basel Framework: OPE25.8 ILM formula, BIC = 0
entry.summary: Reported. The OPE25.8 ILM formula has no rule for BIC equal to zero when a bucket 1 bank is allowed to use loss data.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0397 — Basel Framework: NSF30.32 FAQ1 (footnote number)
entry.summary: Reported. The NSF30.32 FAQ attributes the definition of NSFR derivative liabilities to footnote 18, which holds the RSF formula; the definition is in footnote 2.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0396 — Basel Framework: NSF30.29 FAQ1 vs NSF30.28
entry.summary: Reported. The NSFR FAQ on Level 2A covered bonds says a rating 'above AA–' is required, while NSF30.28 and LCR30.43 accept 'at least AA–', so a covered bond rated exactly AA– gets 15% or 85% RSF depending on which is followed.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0395 — Basel Framework: MAR50.68 Table 10 vs MAR50.66 Table 8
entry.summary: Reported. MAR50.68 Table 10 labels buckets 8, 9 as IG and 16 as HY/NR, contradicting the credit-quality assignment in MAR50.66 Table 8.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0394 — Basel Framework: MAR33.45 k formula
entry.summary: Reported. The surcharge factor k in MAR33.45 divides by the sum of SA charges of green and amber desks and is undefined when that sum is zero.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0393 — Basel Framework: MAR33.42 vs MAR32.9 Table 1
entry.summary: Reported. The MAR32.9 Table 1 header cites MAR33.44 for the qualitative add-on, but that add-on is set in MAR33.42; MAR33.44 covers quarterly updates.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0392 — Basel Framework: MAR33.20 FAQ1 reference to MAR33.28
entry.summary: Reported. FAQ1 to MAR33.20 cites MAR33.28 for the one-year correlation horizon, but that statement is in MAR33.27 (the same FAQ under MAR33.27 cites MAR33.27).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0391 — Basel Framework: MAR33.15 IMCC(C_i)
entry.summary: Reported. IMCC(C_i) in MAR33.15 contains the ratio ES_F,C,i / ES_R,C,i, which has no value for a risk class without positions. The CRR writes the convention out (Article 325bb(3) includes a risk class only where the portfolio has a modellable risk factor in it); the Basel text does not.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0390 — Basel Framework: MAR31.16 Table 1 row (D)
entry.summary: Reported. Row (D) of MAR31.16 Table 1 ends at 0.95 ≤ δ < 1.00, so a delta of exactly 1.00 falls in no bucket.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0389 — Basel Framework: MAR22.39 first sentence
entry.summary: Reported. MAR22.39, in the CTP section, says the maturity scaling and offsetting rules apply to securitisations "(non-CTP)", a label copied from MAR22.30.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0388 — Basel Framework: MAR22.23 HBR; MAR22.44 HBR_ctp
entry.summary: Reported. The hedge benefit ratio in MAR22.23 is not defined when a bucket has no net long and no net short JTD positions, as its denominator is then zero.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0387 — Basel Framework: MAR22.3 range of subsections
entry.summary: Reported. MAR22.3 refers to MAR22.9-MAR22.26 for per-risk-class DRC definitions, a range that covers only non-securitisations while the securitisation rules run to MAR22.45.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0386 — Basel Framework: MAR21.58 FAQ1 vs MAR21.33(1)
entry.summary: Reported. The CTP index FAQ says 'at least 75%' while citing MAR21.33(1), which says 'more than 75%'; exactly 75% gets two different buckets.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0385 — Basel Framework: MAR21.33 and MAR21.38(2) bucket references
entry.summary: Reported. MAR21.33 and MAR21.38 cite MAR21.53 (the CSR risk-weight table) for bucket definitions, which are in MAR21.51.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0384 — Basel Framework: FAQ1 under MAR21.34 vs MAR21.33(1)
entry.summary: Reported. The FAQ to MAR21.34 uses 'at least 75%' for assigning an index CTP to a sector bucket while MAR21.33(1) requires 'more than 75%', so an index at exactly 75% maps differently.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0383 — Basel Framework: MAR21.1 and MAR21.4
entry.summary: Reported. MAR21.1 points to MAR21.8-MAR21.14 (risk-factor definitions) for across-bucket aggregation, which is actually set out in MAR21.4 and MAR21.5.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0382 — Basel Framework: LEV30.3 second example
entry.summary: Reported. LEV30.3 cites CAP10.19 for the IRB provisions-shortfall deduction from CET1, but CAP10.19 covers the opposite case (excess provisions in Tier 2); the deduction is in CAP30.13.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0381 — Basel Framework: LCR40.79 FAQ2 -> LCR40.80
entry.summary: Reported. FAQ2 under LCR40.79 attributes the 0% inflow for firm shorts to LCR40.80, which only sets outflow rates; the inflow rate is in the LCR40.79 table.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0380 — Basel Framework: LCR40.44 reference to LCR40.87
entry.summary: Reported. LCR40.44 sends segregated prime-brokerage balances to LCR40.87 (wholesale loan payments, 50% or 100%), while the rule for such balances sits in LCR40.88, which is optional and conditional on HQLA.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0379 — Basel Framework: LCR31.29
entry.summary: Reported. LCR31.29 points to LCR31.7-31.10 as the jurisdiction's information base, but those paragraphs are bank-to-supervisor usage rules; the shortfall information sits in LCR31.24-31.28.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0378 — Basel Framework: LCR10.9 -> LCR30.29
entry.summary: Reported. LCR10.9 cites LCR30.29 for the single reporting currency requirement, but that requirement sits in LCR30.27; LCR30.29 covers HQLA diversification.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0377 — Basel Framework: CRE54.35 second bullet (holding periods CRE22.61 to CRE22.64)
entry.summary: Reported. CRE54.35 cites CRE22.61 to CRE22.64 for SFT holding periods, but those paragraphs contain none; the holding periods are in CRE22.56 to CRE22.58.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0376 — Basel Framework: CRE54.35 first bullet (haircuts CRE22.44)
entry.summary: Reported. CRE54.35 sends SFT haircuts to CRE22.44, which is the netting-recognition paragraph; the haircut tables are CRE22.49-22.51.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0375 — Basel Framework: CRE54.31 (SFT exposures: CRE22.68 to CRE22.72)
entry.summary: Reported. CRE54.31 points to CRE22.68-22.72 for the SFT exposure, but those paragraphs cover loan/deposit netting and guarantees; the SFT formula is CRE22.65.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0374 — Basel Framework: CRE54.8 bullet 1 (reference to CRE22.61)
entry.summary: Reported. CRE54.8 points to CRE22.61 for the 20-day MPOR floor on netting sets above 5000 trades, but that floor is in CRE22.58.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0373 — Basel Framework: CRE52.59 Step 5
entry.summary: Reported. In the SA-CCR foreign exchange steps, Step 5 sums add-ons 'calculated in step 5', a self-reference; step 4 is meant.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0372 — Basel Framework: CRE52.50
entry.summary: Reported. CRE52.50 defines the margin period of risk by reference to CRE50.18, which defines the margin threshold; the MPOR definition is CRE50.19.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0371 — Basel Framework: CRE52.40 delta, T_i = 0
entry.summary: Reported. The supervisory option delta divides by the square root of the time to exercise and the text gives no floor or rule when that time is zero.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0370 — Basel Framework: CRE52.20 / CRE52.23 multiplier
entry.summary: Reported. The SA-CCR multiplier in CRE52.23 divides by the aggregate add-on, and the text gives no convention for a netting set whose aggregate add-on is zero. Taking the limit gives a potential future exposure of zero.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0369 — Basel Framework: CRE36.31 FAQ2
entry.summary: Reported. FAQ2 under CRE36.31 quotes a sentence of CRE36.30 that is not in CRE36.30 of the published chapter.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0368 — Basel Framework: CRE34.11 reference to CRE44.10
entry.summary: Reported. CRE34.11 points to CRE44.10 for first-loss treatment of collateral and guarantees on purchased receivables, but CRE44.10 only concerns gross-of-provision measurement.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0367 — Basel Framework: CRE33.15 Good vs Satisfactory columns (monitoring)
entry.summary: Reported. The CRE33.15 object-finance monitoring row's Weak cell is garbled ('is able to monitor ... are limited').

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0366 — Basel Framework: CRE33.13 table, Political and legal environment
entry.summary: Reported. The CRE33.13 project-finance slotting table has a row (local content relief) with grade labels instead of criteria and an antecedent-less 'such relief'.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0365 — Basel Framework: CRE32.63 (cross-ref to CRE20.92)
entry.summary: Reported. CRE32.63 refers to CRE20.92 for 100% CCF items, but CRE20.92 is the currency-mismatch multiplier and the 100% CCF list is in CRE20.95.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0364 — Basel Framework: CRE32.10
entry.summary: Reported. The LGD* formula divides by E x (1+H_E), which is zero for an undrawn commitment whose exposure arises only through the CCF.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0363 — Basel Framework: CRE31.2 / CRE32.4
entry.summary: Reported. Sovereign exposures are exempt from the 0.05% PD floor, yet the risk-weight function uses ln(PD) and G(PD), which are undefined at PD = 0.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0362 — Basel Framework: CRE31.6
entry.summary: Reported. CRE31.6 cites CRE32.43-32.54 for effective maturity, but the maturity rules are CRE32.44-32.55, so the cross-reference is off by one at both ends.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0251 — 2 CFR 184.6(a)(8): how does the engineered wood standard implement the statutory requirement for input manufacturing?
entry.summary: Reported. Section 70915(b)(2)(A) of the Build America, Buy America Act directs OMB to ensure that its standards require that each manufacturing process required for the manufacture of the construction material and its inputs occurs in the United States. For engineered wood, 2 CFR 184.6(a)(8) covers all manufacturing processes from the initial combination of constituent materials until the wood product is in its final form. The 2023 preamble says that only the engineered wood standard applies, even though the lumber and polymer standards could otherwise apply, and explains the standard by the manufacturing processes used in the industry. One reading treats the combination of constituents as the starting point OMB chose under its delegated authority. The other asks whether the manufacture of previously manufactured lumber inputs is also required.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0250 — 2 CFR 184.6(a)(4): how does the fiber optic cable standard implement the statutory requirement for input manufacturing?
entry.summary: Reported. Section 70915(b)(2)(A) of the Build America, Buy America Act directs OMB to ensure that its standards require that each manufacturing process required for the manufacture of the construction material and its inputs occurs in the United States. For fiber optic cable, 2 CFR 184.6(a)(4) requires ribboning (where applicable), buffering, fiber stranding and jacketing in the United States. It includes the glass and optical fiber standards and excludes the standards for non-ferrous metals, plastic and polymer-based products, and other materials. The 2023 preamble explains why OMB treated the cable as a single construction material with its own standard. One reading treats the listed processes as the definition Congress delegated to OMB. The other asks whether the manufacture of polymer and other non-fiber inputs before jacketing is also required.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0249 — DFARS 252.225-7052 and 252.225-7961: is there guidance on performance before an existing contract is modified?
entry.summary: Reported. The DPCAP memorandum of October 5, 2026 directs contracting officers to incorporate 252.225-7961 and remove 252.225-7052 in existing contracts as soon as practicable, and not to request consideration when making the modification under FAR 1.107(d). Clause 7052 applies its upstream restriction to deliveries from January 1, 2027. Clause 7961 and the statute as amended by section 848 attach it to contracts awarded on or after that date. One reading keeps the 7052 text binding on performance until the modification is made. The other treats the amended statute and the directed replacement as removing the upstream restriction for contracts awarded before that date.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0248 — DFARS 225.7018-2(a)(2) and clause 252.225-7961: does “mined, refined, or separated” reach ore and feedstock stages?
entry.summary: Reported. For contracts awarded on or after January 1, 2027, Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1, bars covered material “mined, refined, or separated in any covered country”, and clause 252.225-7961 uses the same words. The earlier clause 252.225-7052 described the restriction for each listed material, from mining or production of an ore or feedstock, including recycled material, through finished products. One reading applies the new words to the ore and feedstock stages from which the listed material is made. The other limits them to the listed covered material itself.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0247 — 10 U.S.C. 4872(e): how should a statutory national-security waiver be reflected in clause 252.225-7961?
entry.summary: Reported. Section 4872(e)(1) allows the Secretary to accept delivery of an end item containing covered material manufactured in a covered nation on a written determination that acceptance is necessary to the national security interests of the United States. Paragraph (e)(3) allows a waiver made under 4863(k) to be applied to these restrictions. Case 2024-D014 covers the amendment that made those waivers applicable. The procedure in the deviation and clause 252.225-7961(c) provide for a nonavailability determination and do not describe these waiver paths. One reading lets a valid waiver govern delivery without a change to the clause. The other requires the contract restriction to be modified to reflect it.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0246 — 10 U.S.C. 4872(c)(3)(C): how should the exception for recycled samarium-cobalt magnets be reflected in contracts?
entry.summary: Reported. Section 844(a) of Public Law 119-60 added samarium-cobalt magnets to the exception in 4872(c)(3)(C) for magnets manufactured from recycled material, with milling of the recycled material and sintering of the final magnet in the United States. The deviation and clause 252.225-7961 keep the exception for recycled neodymium-iron-boron magnets only. The clause also states that its restriction on samarium-cobalt magnets is in addition to any applicable specialty metals restriction. Case 2024-D014 includes this amendment. One reading lets a magnet that meets the statutory conditions fall outside the clause now. The other keeps the clause restriction until it is amended, with any specialty metals restriction applying separately.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0245 — 10 U.S.C. 4872(c)(3)(D): how should the exception for recycled tantalum, tungsten and molybdenum be reflected in contracts?
entry.summary: Reported. Section 844(a) of Public Law 119-60 added 4872(c)(3)(D): tantalum, tungsten, or molybdenum produced from recycled material, if the contractor demonstrates to the Secretary that the recycled material was produced outside a covered nation and melting and all further processing and manufacturing take place in the United States or in the country of a qualifying foreign government. When these conditions are met, the prohibition in 4872(a)(1) does not apply. The deviation and clause 252.225-7961 keep only the exception for recycled neodymium-iron-boron magnets. Case 2024-D014 includes this amendment. One reading lets a contractor that meets the statutory conditions rely on the exception now. The other keeps the clause restriction until the clause is amended, because the statutory exception does not by itself establish compliance with the contract.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0244 — Molybdenum in 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(1): what interim contract instructions apply while the DFARS definition is updated?
entry.summary: Reported. Public Law 119-60, section 844(a)(1), added molybdenum to the definition of covered material in 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(1). The DFARS definition in 225.7018-1, the definition in Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1, and clause 252.225-7961 keep the five-material list without molybdenum. DFARS case 2024-D014 already covers this amendment. One view is that the statutory prohibition applies to DoD acquisitions of molybdenum now. The other is that contract obligations follow the clause list, which does not include molybdenum, until the case is completed.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0243 — DFARS 225.7003-3(b)(2)(i)(D)(1): should the COTS fastener exception also list components, as the statute and clause do?
entry.summary: Reported. DFARS 225.7003-3(b)(2)(i)(D)(1) treats commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) fasteners as excepted when they are incorporated into “COTS end items, subsystems, or assemblies”. Clause 252.225-7009(c)(2)(i)(D)(1) and 10 U.S.C. 4863(h)(2)(D)(i) also list components. For example, a separate subcontract supplies COTS fasteners containing specialty metal for a COTS component that will enter a non-COTS end item. One reading applies the narrower list in Part 225 to that acquisition. The other reads Part 225 in line with the statute and the clause.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0242 — FAR 52.225-11(c)(1)(i)(H): should the justification refer to paragraph (b)(4), as the introduction does?
entry.summary: Reported. Under 52.225-11(c)(1)(i), a contractor request to use foreign construction material “in accordance with paragraph (b)(4)” must include listed information. Item (H) asks for a detailed justification of the reason for use of foreign construction materials “cited in accordance with paragraph (b)(3)”. Paragraph (b)(3) is the list of excepted materials. Paragraph (b)(4) states the grounds on which the Contracting Officer may add material to that list. One reading takes (H) to ask for a justification under the grounds in (b)(4). The other takes it to refer to the materials on the (b)(3) list.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0241 — FAR 25.202(a)(2): should the relief from a nonavailability determination state that it applies when the fallback procedures are used?
entry.summary: Reported. FAR 25.202(a)(2) says a nonavailability determination is not required before January 1, 2030, if there is an offer for a foreign construction material that exceeds 55 percent domestic content, with a cross-reference to 25.204(b)(1)(ii) and (b)(2)(ii). Those paragraphs set the fallback procedures and their conditions. The 2022 final rule preamble says the language clarifies that a determination is not required when the fallback procedures are used. One reading applies the sentence whenever such an offer exists. The other reads it, with the cross-reference and the preamble, as limited to cases in which the fallback procedures are used.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0240 — FAR 25.106(c)(1)(ii) and (c)(2)(ii): should the critical-item price tests name the critical calculation expressly?
entry.summary: Reported. For end products that are critical items or contain critical components, 25.106(c)(1)(ii) and (c)(2)(ii) test the price against the low offer after addition of “the appropriate evaluation factor in accordance with paragraph (a) or (b) of this section”. Paragraph (b) gives the factors for end products that are not critical items. Paragraph (a)(1) directs use of the factors in paragraphs (b) and (c), paragraph (c)(1)(i) specifies the critical calculation, and (c)(2)(i)(B) expressly applies the factors in (c)(1). One reading takes the reference through (a) to the critical calculation. The other follows the alternative reference to (b). The FAR Overhaul Part 25 guide keeps the same references.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0239 — FAR 52.225-9(b)(3)(i)(A)(2): should the U.S.-manufacture condition sit on the selected offer, as in Part 25?
entry.summary: Reported. The provisions concern construction material that is not a commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) item and is not wholly or predominantly iron or steel, during the fallback period before January 1, 2030. FAR 25.204(b)(1)(ii) applies when the low offer does not exceed 55 percent domestic content, and treats as domestic the lowest offer that is manufactured in the United States and exceeds 55 percent domestic content. Clause 52.225-9(b)(3)(i)(A)(2) instead requires the low offer to be manufactured in the United States, and treats as domestic the lowest offer above 55 percent without that condition. Clause 52.225-11(b)(4)(i)(A)(2) follows Part 25. One reading applies 52.225-9 as written in contracts that include it. The other reads it in line with Part 25 and 52.225-11.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0238 — FAR 25.205(c): should the minimum consideration for a postaward exception cite 25.204 directly?
entry.summary: Reported. FAR 25.205(c) sets the minimum consideration for a postaward exception based on unreasonable price by reference to the amount “established in 25.202(a) or in accordance with agency procedures”. Paragraph 25.202(a)(3) sets no amount; it points onward to 25.204, which adds 20 percent of the cost of the foreign construction material. Clauses 52.225-9(c)(2) and 52.225-11(c)(2) state their own minimum by reference to the evaluation factor in each clause. One reading takes the reference to 25.202(a) to reach the 25.204 factor through (a)(3). The other reads 25.202(a) as naming no amount, so that the minimum comes from agency procedures or the clause.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0237 — FAR 52.225-9(b)(3)(i) and 52.225-11(b)(4)(i): headings (A) and (B) overlap when a material is a critical item or contains critical components, but not both
entry.summary: Reported. In both clauses, heading (A) covers “domestic construction material that is not a critical item or does not contain critical components”, and heading (B) covers material that “is a critical item or contains critical components”. When exactly one of the two conditions holds, both headings apply. The corresponding heading in FAR 25.204(b)(1) uses “and”: material that “is not a critical item and does not contain critical components”. The list of critical items at 25.105(a)(1)-(2) is reserved.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0236 — FAR 25.101(d)(2)(i) refers to 25.1101(b)(1)(v); paragraph 25.1101(b)(1) ends at (iv)
entry.summary: Reported. FAR 25.101(d)(2)(i) says “See 25.1101(a)(1)(ii) or 25.1101(b)(1)(v) for use of the appropriate Alternate clause”. Paragraph 25.1101(b)(1) ends at (iv), which prescribes Alternate IV for the alternate domestic content test. The FAR Overhaul version refers to 25.601(b)(1)(v), which also ends at (iv).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0235 — FAR 25.1101(b)(1)(iv) refers to 25.102(d); section 25.102 has no paragraph (d)
entry.summary: Reported. FAR 25.1101(b)(1)(iv) applies when the senior procurement executive allows an alternate domestic content test “in accordance with 25.102(d)”. Section 25.102 is a single unnumbered paragraph. The authority for the alternate domestic content test is in 25.101(d). The FAR Overhaul Part 25 text keeps the same reference at 25.601(b)(1)(iv).

entry.summary: Accepted by the addressee. The same 2025 rule replaces the first amount in paragraph (b) with $7,445; this is also the figure its table derives from $7,256. The eCFR shows $7,455 in its versions as of 31 December 2025 and 20 October 2026: the amendment was incorporated with two digits transposed.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0011 — eCFR shows $84,852 in 11 CFR 111.24(a)(2)(ii); the January 2025 rule replaced it with $87,056
entry.summary: Accepted by the addressee. The Federal Election Commission's 2025 inflation adjustment (90 FR 210, FR Doc. 2024-31368) amends section 111.24 by replacing the amount in paragraph (a)(2)(ii) with $87,056. The eCFR still shows the earlier $84,852 in its versions as of 31 December 2025 and 20 October 2026: the amendment to this paragraph was not incorporated.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0007 — 26 U.S.C. §877(a)(2) substitutes “2003” for “1992” in §1(f)(3)(B), which no longer contains “1992”
entry.summary: Editorial note added. Section 877(a)(2) adjusts the $124,000 tax-liability threshold for expatriates by the cost-of-living adjustment under section 1(f)(3) “by substituting ‘2003’ for ‘1992’ in subparagraph (B) thereof”. Section 1(f)(3)(B) no longer contains “1992”, so the substitution finds nothing to replace. The threshold is still used: §877A defines a covered expatriate through §877(a)(2).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0006 — 26 U.S.C. §642(b)(2)(C)(iii)(II) indexes “the $4,150 amount in subparagraph (A)”, which holds $100
entry.summary: Editorial note added. Subclause (II) increases “the $4,150 amount in subparagraph (A)” for inflation. Subparagraph (A) of §642(b)(2) contains $100; the $4,150 amount is in subclause (I) of the same clause, which substitutes it for the exemption amount while that amount is zero.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0005 — 26 U.S.C. §42(j)(5)(C)(i) refers to “subparagraph (B)(i)”, which has had no clauses since 1988
entry.summary: Editorial note added. Section 42(j)(5)(C)(i) treats a husband and wife as one partner “for purposes of subparagraph (B)(i)”. Subparagraph (B) is a single sentence about partnerships with 35 or more partners and has had no clauses since P.L. 100-647 §4004(a) rewrote it.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0004 — 26 U.S.C. §42(i)(3)(C)(ii) defines a related person by reference to “subsection (d)(2)(D)(iii)”, which no longer exists
entry.summary: Editorial note added. Section 42(i)(3)(C)(ii) excludes units owned by a person “related (as defined in subsection (d)(2)(D)(iii))” to the occupant. P.L. 110-289 §3003(e) and (g)(2) redesignated that definition as subsection (d)(2)(D)(ii), which now reads “(ii) Related person”; subparagraph (D) has no clause (iii).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0003 — 26 U.S.C. §42(e)(3)(B) refers to “subsection (b)(2)(B)(ii)”, which no longer exists
entry.summary: Editorial note added. Section 42(e)(3)(B) sets the credit for certain rehabilitation expenditures “using the percentage applicable under subsection (b)(2)(B)(ii)”. Subsection (b)(2)(B) has had no clauses since P.L. 110-289 §3002(a) restructured subsection (b); the 30 percent rule is now in subsection (b)(1)(B)(ii). The reference was not conformed when subsection (b) was rewritten.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0217 — aifc.kz page of the Regulations on Damages and Remedies sends readers for the 'current version' to the AFSA Auditor Rules
entry.summary: Reported. Under "Effective Version" the aifc.kz page of the AIFC Regulations on Damages and Remedies states "current version can be found on Regulator's website:" and links https://orderly.myafsa.com/articles/auditorrules. That section of the AFSA rulebook is the AIFC Auditor Rules. The Regulations on Damages and Remedies (No. 17 of 2017) are not an AFSA rulebook. The same link appears on the aifc.kz page of the Auditor Rules. The only PDF offered is the 2017 text.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0216 — Recognition of arbitral awards: Article 14(4) of the Constitutional Statute and Article 45(1) of the Arbitration Regulations; the English translation of Article 14(4) is narrower than the Russian and Kazakh texts
entry.summary: Reported. Article 14(4) of the Constitutional Statute (Russian and Kazakh texts) provides that recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards on the territory of the Centre follow the legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan. The English translation on aifc.kz reads "Awards of arbitration courts in the Republic of Kazakhstan", which is narrower. Article 45(1) of the AIFC Arbitration Regulations provides for recognition and enforcement by the AIFC Court of an award "irrespective of the State or jurisdiction in which it was made". The structure of Article 14 supports the narrower reading; on it, the two rules overlap only for awards made in Kazakhstan outside the AIFC. We do not claim that Article 45 cannot be applied.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0215 — Arbitration Regulations Art. 9(2): for foreign-seated arbitrations Articles 17 and 18 apply, but not Article 16 (stay of court proceedings)
entry.summary: Reported. Article 9(2) of the AIFC Arbitration Regulations applies "Articles 17, 18, Part 3, and the Schedule" where the seat is outside the AIFC. Article 16 (what the AIFC Court must do when an action is brought in a matter that is subject to an arbitration agreement) is not listed. In the UNCITRAL Model Law (article 1(2)) the corresponding articles 8 and 9 apply whatever the place of arbitration. The AIFC Court can still stay proceedings under its general powers (section 27(2)(g) of the Court Regulations, rule 8.8 of the Court Rules), so the question is whether the Article 16 rule is meant to apply as well.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0214 — IAC Rules 2022: Article 1.4 still gives 1 January 2018 as the commencement date, and the 2022 edition does not say from when its changes apply
entry.summary: Reported. The IAC Arbitration and Mediation Rules 2022 say in Article 1.4 that they "shall come into force on 1 January 2018" and apply to arbitrations commenced on or after that date. The 2022 text was approved by the Chairman of the IAC on 19 September 2022, but it does not say from when its changes apply. Article 2.2 refers to the rules "in force at the date of the commencement of the arbitration", so the parties need that date to know which edition governs.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0213 — IAC Rules 3.2 calculate periods in "Alma-Ata Time (UTC+6)" by default; Kazakhstan has used UTC+5 since 1 March 2024
entry.summary: Reported. Article 3.2: "Unless the Registrar or Tribunal provide otherwise, or unless the parties agree otherwise", "any period of time is to be calculated in accordance with Alma-Ata Time (UTC+6)". Since 1 March 2024 the whole of Kazakhstan uses UTC+5 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 20 of 19 January 2024). Alma-Ata local time and UTC+6 now differ by one hour, so the default end of a day differs too (midnight local time is 01:00 UTC+6). The Registrar may extend time limits (Article 3.8), which reduces the practical effect.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0212 — IAC Rules: two Articles are numbered 7.4; the second refers to "Articles 7.3 and 7.4"
entry.summary: Reported. Article 7.4 (objection that the Tribunal is exceeding the scope of its authority) is followed by a second Article 7.4 ("The Tribunal may rule on an objection referred to in Articles 7.3 and 7.4 ..."). By the word "objection" the reference is to the first 7.4, but any citation of "Article 7.4" is ambiguous. The unofficial Russian translation numbers the second one 7.5.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0211 — IAC Rules 10.7 give 'seven days' to apply to the AIFC Court on a rejected challenge; Arbitration Regulations 22(3), which parties cannot cut, give thirty
entry.summary: Reported. IAC Rules 10.7: a decision rejecting a challenge is "without prejudice to any right a party may have to apply within seven days to the AIFC Court under the Arbitration Regulations, Article 22(3)". Article 22(3) of the Arbitration Regulations gives the challenging party "thirty days after having received notice of the decision rejecting the challenge", and Article 22(1) makes any procedure agreed by the parties subject to paragraph (3). The AIFC Court Rules (rule 27.28) also fix 30 days for this application. Because rule 10.7 is "without prejudice to any right", the 30 days are not cut, but the Rules state the wrong period. The unofficial Russian translation also says "в течение семи дней" (within seven days).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0209 — Court Regulations s.13: the Chief Justice appoints temporary Judges; the Statute (art. 13(3-1), from 2018) reserves appointment of judges to the President
entry.summary: Reported. Section 13(1) of the AIFC Court Regulations lets the Chief Justice, after consulting the Governor, appoint a person as a temporary Judge "to facilitate the disposal of business in the Court"; section 13(3) treats that person "for all purposes" as a Judge. The Regulations were adopted on 5 December 2017 under Article 13(5) of the Constitutional Statute (section 2). At that time Article 13(5) left to the Council resolution on the Court "the procedure for the appointment and removal of judges and other officials of the court". Constitutional Law No. 119-VI of 22 December 2017 added Article 13(3-1): the Chairman and judges of the Centre's court are appointed and released by the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan on the recommendation of the Governor. The same law deleted the words "judges and other" from Article 13(5), so the Council resolution now sets the procedure only for officials of the court. Section 12(1) of the Regulations follows Article 13(3-1) for permanent Judges; section 13 was not aligned. As written, a person appointed under section 13 would hear cases and sign judgments as a Judge without the appointment that Article 13(3-1) requires. We found no sign that section 13 has been used: the judges named in the judgments published on court.aifc.kz since April 2019 are all among the Chief Justice and Justices listed by the Court.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0208 — Court Regulations s.29(2) restates Article 13(6) of the Constitutional Statute as "shall be guided by decisions"; Article 13(6) says the Court may take into account final decisions
entry.summary: Reported. Section 29(2) of the AIFC Court Regulations says that the Court, "as provided by Article 13(6)" of the Constitutional Statute, "shall be guided by decisions of the Court and decisions made in other common law jurisdictions". Article 13(6) is permissive and limited to final decisions: the Court "может учитывать вступившие в законную силу решения" (may take into account final decisions). Being guided is not the same as being bound, so we do not see a clear conflict, but the restatement is not exact.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0207 — Court Rules fix filing and service cut-off at '4pm Alma Ata time (UTC + 6)'; Kazakhstan has used UTC+5 since 1 March 2024
entry.summary: Reported. Rule 2.12 requires any act due "on or before a particular date" to be done "by 4pm Alma Ata time (UTC + 6)", and rule 5.15 treats a document "delivered before 4pm Alma Ata time (UTC + 6) on a business day" as served that day. When the Rules were written both labels meant the same time. Since 1 March 2024 the whole of Kazakhstan uses the fifth time zone, UTC+5 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 20 of 19 January 2024, amending Resolution No. 1749 of 23 November 2000). Since then "Alma Ata time" and "UTC + 6" differ by one hour: 4pm UTC+6 is 3pm local time, and 4pm local time is 5pm UTC+6.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0206 — Court Rules r.28.7: 'Part 23 (judgments and orders)' applies to small claims, but Part 23 is the Abridged Procedure; judgments and orders are Part 24
entry.summary: Reported. Rule 28.7(9) lists "Part 23 (judgments and orders)" among the provisions that apply to small claims. Part 23 is "Abridged Procedure for Claims"; "Judgments and Orders" is Part 24. The words in brackets are part of the rule. The unofficial Russian translation repeats "Часть 23 (судебные решения и приказы)", while its own contents name Part 24 "Судебные решения и приказы".

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0205 — DP Rules Schedule 1: the 50% fee reduction for 1 March 2025 - 1 March 2026 appears only in a "Note", which is not part of the act
entry.summary: Reported. Under the fees table of Schedule 1 (items 2 and 3) the 2025 consolidation adds: "Note: For the period commencing on 1 March 2025 and concluding on 1 March 2026, the fees under items 2 and 3 of the Table of fee are applied with 50% reduction." Under section 26(1)(a) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts a note is not part of the act, and under section 27 a note is merely explanatory. Rule 7.2 and the table still set the full amounts. The amending instrument of 2025 is not on the act page, so we could not see whether it contains an operative rule for the reduction. The period ended on 1 March 2026.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0204 — DP Rules r.4.2.3(a): first notification due 'no later than 14 days start of the operations' - before or after the start is not said
entry.summary: Reported. Rule 4.2.3(a) requires the notification of Personal Data Processing operations 'no later than 14 days start of the operations' - a word ('after' or 'before') is missing, so the deadline can be read as 14 days before the operations start or 14 days after. The neighbouring r.4.3 uses the full form 'no later than 14 days after the day the particulars change'. Text unchanged since the 2018 Rules; the notification attracts the item 3 fee (USD 1,000/500/200).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0203 — s.16-2(7) points to 'measures referred to in section 24-1(1) and 24-1(2)'; s.24-1 contains no measures
entry.summary: Reported. Section 16-2(7): adherence by a Processor or Sub-processor to an approved certification mechanism "may demonstrate the sufficiency of the measures referred to in section 24-1(1) and 24-1(2)". Section 24-1(1) allows a certification scheme to be established; section 24-1(2) says certification does not relieve responsibility. None of them refers to any measures. The assurances and measures of processors and sub-processors are dealt with in section 16-2(1), (2) and (3).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0202 — Data Protection Regulations s.9: the lawful-basis rule is addressed to the Data Processor, while other sections treat it as the Data Controller's basis - who is bound?
entry.summary: Reported. Section 9 of the Data Protection Regulations opens "A Data Processor must not Process Personal Data unless" one of grounds (a)-(e) applies. The grounds themselves refer to the Data Controller, and sections 9-1(1), 13(1)(c)(v) and 14(2)(c)(v) treat section 9 as the Controller's lawful basis. The Controller's duty to process lawfully also follows from section 8(1)(a). A Processor may well be meant to be bound too, so the text allows more than one reading of who is bound by section 9. For comparison, the corresponding ADGM provision (Data Protection Regulations 2015, section 2) opened without naming an addressee: "Personal Data may only be Processed if".

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0201 — DP Regulations 2025: section 9-2 'Right to withdraw consent' is listed and cited twice but has no text
entry.summary: Reported. Section 9-1(5) twice refers to section 9-2: the right to withdraw consent "afforded ... under section 9-2" and the duty to inform the Data Subject "how to exercise it as set out in section 9-2". The contents list "9-2. Right to withdraw consent", but the text passes from section 9-1(12) directly to section 10. Section 9-1(5) itself says that consent may be withdrawn at any time, that withdrawing must be at least as easy as giving consent and that it does not affect earlier processing; section 9-1(9) requires procedures for recording withdrawal. The amending instrument of 1 April 2025 is not on the act page, so it cannot be established whether the instrument or the consolidation lost section 9-2.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0200 — Foreign-labour record rules (2018) put the reporting duty on the foreign employee; Article 8(3) of the Constitutional Statute, as amended in December 2019, names AIFC Participants and bodies
entry.summary: Reported. Article 8(3) of the Constitutional Statute, as amended by Constitutional Law No. 296-VI of 30 December 2019, requires Participants and bodies of the Centre to submit information on attracted foreign nationals to the AIFC Authority "in accordance with acts of the Centre". The only implementing act we found, AIFC Rules No. 2 of 2018 (rule 2.2), puts the duty on the Foreign Employee, who may file in person or through the Employer. The two duties can coexist, but we found no act of the Centre addressed to Participants and bodies. Rule 2.2 also uses "admit" where "apply" or "submit" seems meant.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0199 — Employment Regulations s.26: rest breaks of "not less than 15 hours" for a working day of more than 6 hours
entry.summary: Reported. Section 26 of the Employment Regulations entitles an Employee whose working time on a day is more than 6 hours to rest breaks of "not less than 15 hours" in total; the breaks "may be spent away from the Employee's workstation". With the 8-hour limit in section 24 this makes a day of 23 hours of work and breaks, and more than 24 hours once working time exceeds 9 hours, so the figure is hard to apply as a break during work. The text has been the same since 2017. For comparison, the ADGM Employment Regulations (2015, 2019 and 2024), which have the same structure and the same 6-hour trigger, give rest breaks of not less than 1 hour in aggregate. The intended figure cannot be derived from the AIFC text itself.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0198 — Consolidated V3 and V4 of the Employment Regulations drop the text of section 65-1 (Whistleblowing); only the contents entry remains
entry.summary: Reported. Version 2 of the Employment Regulations (amendments as of 22 February 2019) contains Part 10-1 with section 65-1, which extends to Employees the whistleblower protections of Part 14-2 of the Companies Regulations. The later amending instruments on the act page (No. 30 of 2019 and No. 39 of 2021) do not omit it. Yet the consolidated V3 and the current V4 list "PART 10-1: WHISTLEBLOWING" in the contents but have no text for it. The full text on the aifc.kz website goes from Part 10 to Part 11 and has no Part 10-1 and no section 65-1. The act page publishes no instrument that inserted section 65-1 in February 2019, and no instrument that omitted it. Part 14-2 of the Companies Regulations still protects any Worker directly.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0194 — ITRP Regulations (AIFC Regulations No. 57 of 2026): "Tax Code" is the repealed Code No. 120-VI in the English and Kazakh texts, and sections 29(2) and 30(2) restate rules that current law no longer contains
entry.summary: Reported. AIFC Regulations No. 57 of 2026 on the AIFC Investment Tax Residency Programme (6 August 2026) replaced AIFC Act No. 42 of 2022 (section 3). The English and Kazakh texts of its Schedule define "Tax Code" as the Code of 25 December 2017 No. 120-VI, which was repealed on 1 January 2026. The Russian text gives only the name of the Code, without a date or number; under Article 2(5) of the Tax Code of 18 July 2025 No. 214-VIII that name now refers to the current Code, so the language versions point to different Codes. Sections 29(2) and 30(2), carried over from Act No. 42 word for word, restate rules of Article 218(2) of the 2017 Code: the investment resident provides, "along with other documents determined by the Tax Code", the AIFC Authority's confirmation letter, and the residency certificate "is issued for the year in which the fee ... was paid". Under the 2025 Code these documents are no longer in the Code: Article 224(1) leaves the procedure to the authorised body, and the list for an AIFC investment resident, including the confirmation letter, is in item 8(6) of the list of requirements to the Rules approved by Order of the Minister of Finance of 11 November 2025 No. 689. The 2025 Code and Order No. 689 do not keep the fee-year rule: Article 224(3)(3) confirms residency for the calendar year stated in the application and Article 224(4) for the past and (or) the current year. For example, an investor who pays the fee in January 2026 and asks for confirmation for 2025 would get a certificate for 2026 under section 30(2), while Article 224(4) allows 2025. Sections 29(1) and 30(1) refer to the acting tax legislation, so residency itself follows current law, but section 30(2) states a period that current law does not set.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0191 — aifc.kz: the page of the CIT/VAT-exempt List sends readers for the 'current version' to the regulator's page of a different act — the AML list of services subject to financial monitoring
entry.summary: Reported. The aifc.kz page "The List of financial services provided by the AIFC participants, income from which is exempt from CIT and VAT" (Joint Order No. 126/547/118 of 2020) says that the current version can be found on the regulator's website and links to orderly.myafsa.com/articles/the-list-of-financial-services-and-ancillary-services-...-subject-to-the-financial-monitoring. That address is the regulator's page of a different act: the list of services subject to financial monitoring, which aifc.kz publishes on its own page with the same link.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0188 — NPIO Regulations Schedule 1: "Authorised Activities" defined by s.8, which is the prohibition; the definition is in s.9
entry.summary: Reported. The definition reads "section 8 (Authorised Activities of Incorporated Organisations)". s.8 is "Prohibition against conducting certain activities". s.9 is "Authorised Activities of Incorporated Organisations", and s.9(2) lists them. The heading in brackets saves the meaning. The NPIO Rules fine table correctly cites "9(1) Authorised Activities".

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0187 — Foundations Regulations s.14(1)(g): UBO particulars "required by Part 16" of the Companies Regulations; that Part is 14-1 (Part 16 does not exist)
entry.summary: Reported. Companies Regulations V8 end with Part 15. The UBO Part was renumbered from 16 to 14-1 by A2, in force 01.03.2019. The Foundations Regulations, adopted after that (26.03.2019), cite "Part 16 (Ultimate Beneficial Owners)" in s.14(1)(g). The same act cites "Part 14-1 (Ultimate Beneficial Owners)" in its application section near the end. The heading in brackets saves the meaning.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0186 — Foundations Regulations s.36: since Amendments No. 1 (2019) "the Foundation's return date" is not defined; since Amendments No. 3 (2023) s.36(4)-(5) still refer to "Schedule 3 (Fines and Fees)" and to fees "prescribed in Regulations"
entry.summary: Reported. Amendments No. 1 to the Foundations Regulations (2019) deleted the definition of the return date ("each anniversary of the date it received its Commercial Licence") from section 36(3) but kept the words "made up to the Foundation's return date"; the term is not defined elsewhere. The filing deadline, "within 6 months of the end of each financial year", does not depend on that date, and the Registrar may set another date. Amendments No. 3 (2023) moved fees to the Fees Rules (section 61) and removed fees from Schedule 3, but section 36(4) still refers to "Schedule 3 (Fines and Fees)" and section 36(5) still requires "application for registration fees ... as prescribed in Regulations".

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0185 — Foundations Regulations Schedule 3: fine row "6(6)" for failing to give a copy of an assignment; the duty and the fine are in s.6(7)
entry.summary: Reported. Row "6(6) Person failing to provide a copy of assignment of rights - 1,500". s.6(6) only permits assignment of rights if the By-laws allow. The duty to give the Registrar a copy within 30 days, with "liable to a fine, as set out in Schedule 3", is s.6(7). Amendments No. 3 (2023) itself quotes 6(7) as the fine provision. The description in the row matches 6(7).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0184 — Insolvency Regulations ss.98-99: where inability to pay is proved to the Court, which date is the "onset of Insolvency"?
entry.summary: Reported. Sections 98 and 99 of the Insolvency Regulations measure look-back periods to "the onset of Insolvency". For Part 10, Schedule 3 defines "Insolvency" as being Unable to Pay its Debts, the approval of a Voluntary Arrangement or the appointment of a Receiver or Administrative Receiver. Where inability to pay is "proved to the satisfaction of the Court" (section 50(1)(c) and (2)), the text does not say whether the onset is the date the inability began or the date of the Court's finding; section 98(c) points to the order date for one case only. For comparison, the corresponding ADGM provision (Insolvency Regulations 2015, section 259(3)) defines the onset of insolvency in a separate subsection by reference to formal events.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0183 — Insolvency Regulations s.88(2): the Rules may vary "requirements mentioned in subsection (2)", i.e. in the power itself; the criteria are in (1)
entry.summary: Reported. Section 88(1) says the Rules must prescribe the criteria for registration as an insolvency practitioner or official liquidator. Section 88(2) lets the Rules vary "requirements mentioned in subsection (2)" for applicants regulated outside the AIFC. Subsection (2) is the power itself and mentions no requirements; the criteria are in (1). The parallel provision for auditors, section 134(3) of the Companies Regulations, refers to the subsection that sets the criteria.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0182 — Insolvency Rules, rule 9.1: the consolidated PDFs on aifc.kz number its subrules 8.1.1-8.1.6, while 8.1.1(b) and 9.3.1(a) cite "9.1.3"
entry.summary: Reported. Amendments No. 1 to the Insolvency Rules (2 December 2018) inserted rule 9.1 with subrules 9.1.1-9.1.6. The consolidated PDFs on aifc.kz (V2 and the current V3) print them as 8.1.1-8.1.6, while 8.1.1(b) and 9.3.1(a) still cite "9.1.3". The Insolvency Rules on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) number them 9.1.1-9.1.6, so the cited subrule exists there.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0181 — Companies Regulations Schedule 1 and NPIO Regulations s.33(5): "Objectives" of the Registrar defined by s.9(1) of the Companies Regulations; the objectives are in s.10(1)
entry.summary: Reported. Both definitions point to "section 9(1) (Registrar's Objectives and Functions)". s.9 is "Appointment of Registrar". The objectives are set in s.10(1) ("(the Registrar's Objectives)"), whose heading is the one in brackets. The bracketed heading saves the meaning.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0180 — Companies Rules Schedule 3, items 62 and 64: "179-4(8) or (21)" and "179-7(2) or (15)" name the "in Writing" subsections; the fine clauses of these regimes are 179-4(22) and 179-7(16)
entry.summary: Reported. Schedule 3 of the Companies Rules sets fine limits by naming provisions of the Companies Regulations. Items 62 ("179-4(8) or (21)") and 64 ("179-7(2) or (15)") first appear in V4 (in force 1 January 2020); V3 had only "179-4(8)" and "179-7(2)". Subsections 179-4(21) and 179-7(15) only require notices to be "in Writing", while the fine clauses for these regimes are 179-4(22) and 179-7(16). The same change added "52(17)", also a fine clause, to item 18, so (21) and (15) look off by one. No published amending act contains this change. The Companies Rules on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) have the same text. Whether items 62 and 64 set a limit for breaches of 179-4(9)-(20) and 179-7(3)-(14) depends on how the description in column 3 is read.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0179 — Companies Regulations ss.179-6(1) and 179-7: after Amendments No. 4 moved the Nominee Director particulars to 179-7(1-1), the references in 179-6(1) and in the fine clause 179-7(2) were not updated
entry.summary: Reported. Amendments No. 4 moved the particulars of the Register of Nominee Directors from section 179-7(1) into a new subsection (1-1). Section 179-6(1) still refers to "section 179-7(1)(a) to (e)", and section 179-7(2) still makes only "subsection (1)" finable. Section 21(2) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts allows both references to be read as reaching the moved list, so this is a matter of clarity rather than a gap.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0178 — Companies Rules 5.3 (transfer out of the AIFC): since V4 the subrules are numbered 5.3.3-5.3.6, and three cross-references, including the 60-day notice, point to numbers that no longer exist
entry.summary: Reported. In the Companies Rules V1-V3, rule 5.3 has 5.3.1 (application, with (c) "a declaration ... under subrule 5.3.3"), 5.3.2, 5.3.3 ("For rule 5.3.1(c), the declaration ... must state") and 5.3.4 (60-day notice before "an application mentioned in subrule 5.3.1"). From V4 (in force 1 January 2020) the same subrules are numbered 5.3.3-5.3.6 and there is no 5.3.1 or 5.3.2, but the text is unchanged. So 5.3.3(c) now points to itself, 5.3.5 points to "5.3.1(c)" and 5.3.6 ties the 60-day notice to "an application mentioned in subrule 5.3.1". The Companies Rules on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) have the same numbering. No published amending act changes rule 5.3. Rule 5.3 deals with one application only, so the meaning can be recovered.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0177 — Companies Regulations s.26(4): the fine clause was not updated when Amendments No. 4 moved the annual-return deadline and contents into a new subsection (1-1)
entry.summary: Reported. Amendments No. 4 moved the annual-return deadline and contents from section 26(1) of the Companies Regulations into a new subsection (1-1). Section 26(4) still makes "subsection (1), (2-1) or (3)" punishable by a fine, and item 10 of Schedule 3 of the Companies Rules still says "26(1) or (3)". The reference to (1) may be read as reaching the re-enacted duty (section 21(2) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts), but a reader of section 26(4) cannot see that late or incomplete filing is finable. Item 10 also does not list subsection (2-1), which section 26(4) makes finable.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0176 — Companies Regulations s.26(1-1)(c): annual return takes director particulars from s.13(4)(j), which is the UBO item; directors are in s.13(4)(h)
entry.summary: Reported. s.26(1-1)(c) requires "the particulars mentioned in section 13(4)(j) (Formation of companies) for each Director and, if applicable, the Secretary". s.13(4)(j) is "the particulars required by Part 14-1 (Ultimate Beneficial Owners)". The directors and secretary item is s.13(4)(h): "the full name ..., nationality, address, business occupation (if any) and date of birth of the individuals who are to serve as the Directors and, if applicable, the Secretary". The words "for each Director and, if applicable, the Secretary" fit only (h).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0175 — Companies Regulations s.26-1(2)(b): the confirmation statement covers duties "mentioned in subsection (2)", but the duties are listed in (3)
entry.summary: Reported. Section 26-1(2)(b) requires a statement that all information required "under any duty mentioned in subsection (2)" has been delivered. Subsection (2) is the provision itself and mentions no duty. The list of duties ("The following duties require notification in Writing:") is subsection (3). Subsection (1) is the election, and the only list of duties follows in (3), so the reference reads as written for a text in which the list was subsection (2). The wording has been the same since Amendments No. 4 (in force 1 January 2020).

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0174 — Companies Regulations s.92: the consolidated PDFs on aifc.kz make the fine clause refer to itself; Amendments No. 2 and the AFSA online text number it correctly
entry.summary: Reported. In Amendments No. 2 to the Companies Regulations (in force 1 March 2019) section 92 has subsections (3) on the periods of a disqualification order, (4) "A Person must not Contravene an order under subsection (2)" and (5) "Contravention of subsection (4) is punishable by a fine." The consolidated PDF versions on aifc.kz from V3 to the current V8 drop the number (3). The text of (3) runs on as part of (2), the prohibition becomes (3), and the fine clause, now numbered (4), reads "Contravention of subsection (4)", so in these PDFs it refers to itself. The Companies Regulations on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) keep the numbering (3), (4) and (5) as adopted, so the problem is limited to the aifc.kz PDFs.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0173 — Capital of Digital Asset Service Providers: DAA Table 2 and PRU (INV) Table 3.3 both apply to the same activities with different amounts
entry.summary: Reported. DAA 3.2(1)(b) and Table 2 set the capital of a Digital Asset Service Provider at USD 250,000 for Providing Custody, USD 100,000 for Managing Investments and USD 250,000 for Dealing in Investments as Principal (other than matched principal). PRU (INV) 1.3 applies to any firm authorised to conduct these activities; Investments include Digital Assets (Glossary), and PRU (INV) 1.3(6) does not exclude Digital Asset Business. PRU (INV) Table 3.3 sets USD 500,000 for Providing Custody Services and for Dealing in Investments as Principal and USD 150,000 for Managing Investments, with the liquid assets requirement in PRU (INV) 4. DAA 3.2(1)(a) keeps the general authorisation requirements of other applicable rules, and for stablecoin issuers DAA 4.2(b) states that "the highest amount applies" where another activity requires more capital, so the DAA amounts may be meant as a floor next to PRU (INV). The Rules do not say so for Table 2. Example: a firm licensed only to provide custody of Digital Assets with capital resources of USD 300,000 meets Table 2, but is USD 200,000 below PRU (INV) Table 3.3 for the same activity.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0172 — Unclear application of the Client Money Rules to fiat currency held for Clients in Digital Asset Business
entry.summary: Reported. The Glossary defines Investment Business as a list of activities (a) to (k), "but not including Digital Asset Business", and Digital Asset Business includes Operating a Digital Asset Trading Facility and the other activities in relation to Digital Assets. COB 8.1.4 requires compliance with the Client Money Rules (COB 8.2) by a firm that holds Money for a Client "in the course of, or in connection with, the carrying on of Investment Business or Provides Money Services", and COB 8.2.1 defines Client Money by Investment Business. A Digital Asset Trading Facility Operator holds fiat currency for its Clients (DAA 2.13.4(2): a trade only if there are "sufficient Fiat Currencies or Digital Assets … in the Client's account"). Digital Assets of the same Clients "must be held on trust" (DAA 2.13.7(2), 3.7.1(3)), but no rule says the same of their fiat currency. The Rules of cooperation with second-tier banks require a Digital Asset Service Provider to hold Clients' money and its own money in separate accounts (rule 2.2.3), and DAA 2.13.7(7)(a) requires "segregation and portability arrangements". COB chapter 8 is listed among the applicable provisions only in Guidance to DAA chapters 2 and 3. It is therefore unclear whether this fiat currency is Client Money, whether the Client Money Distribution Rules in COB 8.2.16 apply to it if the firm fails (COB 8.1.2(c) brings in chapter 8 for a firm that Provides Custody, but not for a trading facility that uses a third-party wallet provider or for a broker), and whether it is Excluded Property under Schedule 4 of the Insolvency Rules. Example: a client deposits 20,000 USD with a Digital Asset Trading Facility Operator that uses a third-party wallet provider; the money is held in a separate account under rule 2.2.3; if the operator fails with a shortfall in that account, the Rules do not say how the shortfall is shared.

entry.title: ARXO-2026-0171 — DAA 4.7: the reserve of a Fiat stablecoin is only operationally segregated; the Rules do not say whether it is protected from the issuer's own creditors and how it is shared among holders on insolvency
entry.summary: Reported. DAA 4.7.1(4) requires the issuer of a Fiat stablecoin to ensure that the reserve of assets is "operationally segregated from the proprietary assets of the issuer". DAA 4.7.3(7) requires the custody arrangements to protect the reserve against "claims of the custodian's creditors", and DAA 4.7.3(1)(a) requires that the reserve is "not encumbered nor pledged as Collateral". DAA 4.11.2(1) requires the issuer to grant holders redemption rights "on the reserve assets when the issuer is not able to comply with its obligations", while DAA 4.5(1)(c) speaks of "the rights or the absence of rights granted to the holders". The DAA, PMS and COB do not state that the reserve is held on trust for holders or is otherwise outside the issuer's estate. Under the Insolvency Regulations (Schedule 3) property of a company excludes only property held on trust, and under rule 5.46.1 of the Insolvency Rules unsecured debts rank equally.
